commands.speak: A single one of these cells can run from your spine to your big toe — about a metre of one cell.
These branches are the dendrites: the listening end, collecting signals from thousands of other neurons.
They all feed into the cell body, the soma, which keeps the cell alive and adds the incoming signals up.
If the total crosses a threshold, the neuron fires — all or nothing, never half a signal.
The firing travels out along the axon, the single long output cable.
And it only ever runs one way: in at the dendrites, out along the axon.
These fatty sleeves are myelin, wrapped around the axon with bare gaps between them — the nodes of Ranvier.
The signal cannot leak through the sleeves, so it jumps from gap to gap instead of crawling along.
That jumping is the difference between about one metre per second and a hundred.
At the far end the axon splits into terminals, each ending in a small swelling.
And here the wire stops: the terminal never touches the next cell.
It squirts neurotransmitter across a gap twenty nanometres wide, and the next cell's dendrites listen.
So a neuron is one cell doing four jobs in a row: listen, decide, transmit, and hand over chemically to the next.
